Senses.Note: The primary sense is the shared phrase in the historical Baizhang public case, not a Baizhang-specific meaning. The fox-body sequence is translated because the record literally states it; no broader account is inferred from it. Wansong's contrast, the embedded monk's objection, Wumen's paired verdict, Chaozong's no-rope rebuke, and later same-or-different questions are preserved as speaker-owned positions. They do not create different referents and therefore do not justify a sense split.

Senses.Explanation: In the wild-fox case, 'not obscuring cause and effect' is Baizhang's turning answer; later comments question the fox's release and refuse to isolate it from the rejected companion phrase. The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing deployments and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.
